column4: The contents of the graves are scattered out, directly continuing the section's grave-ground image into bodily exposure at judgment.
The crow scratches the earth to show Cain how to cover his brother's corpse, supplying the Quran's first concrete scene of a human body being put into the ground.
Worldly rivalry continues until people visit the graves; bodily arrival in cemetery-ground terminates the self-exalting contest.
God begins creation, repeats it, and then people are returned to Him, compressing first formation, re-formation, and final return into one ayah.
The return of all to God is guaranteed because He begins and repeats creation; the repeated creation then separates righteous believers' reward from deniers' punishment.
God gives life to the dead, causes death, gives life again, and to Him people are returned; the whole bodily circuit belongs to one sustaining hand.
God promises to repeat creation just as He began the first creation, making the second formation answer directly to the first well-formed body.
إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ يُبْدِئُ وَيُعِيدُ attributes both origination and repetition to the same agent, a compact statement of the section's creation-return relation.
When skeptics ask who will restore them, the answer is the One who formed them the first time; first bodily formation is the warrant for return.
At death the human asks, 'My Lord, return me,' making r-d-d's restoration sense a desperate bodily request at the point of collapse.
The requested return is refused, a barrier remains until resurrection, and the speaker's wish to do righteousness connects bodily return with the faithful exception.
God takes souls at death and sleep, retains those decreed to die, and sends the others back for a term; the same hand withholds and restores bodily life.
The human was first a discharged drop, supplying the low material beginning for the created and proportioned body in 75:38.
After recalling first formation, the passage asks whether its Maker can revive the dead; fine form becomes the direct proof of re-formation.
The question asks the human what deceived him concerning his generous Lord, framing the bodily forming in 82:7-8 and denial in 82:9 as one rebuke.
After creating and proportioning in 87:2, God measures and guides; fitting form is joined to an assigned measure and course.
God has created people in successive stages, supplying the developmental movement between earthly origin and the return-and-emergence of 71:17-18.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay, giving the formed body in 23:14 its material origin in earth.
The drop is placed in a firm lodging, a concrete support and enclosure within the process that produces the completed body in 23:14.
The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it moves the section's fitted form inward, from bodily balance to the human self.
The proportioned self is shown both its wickedness and its piety, explaining how one created form opens toward opposed moral ranks.
Success belongs to the one who purifies the proportioned self, a close ethical counterpart to the section's faithful exception.
Failure belongs to the one who corrupts or buries the self, giving the moral fall an earthward verb after the self's proportioning.
God brings people from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and grants hearing, sight, and hearts, yet little gratitude follows; bestowed equipment can end in moral failure.
God produces human hearing, sight, and hearts, followed by 'little are you grateful'; completed capacities do not guarantee an upright response.
The Creator produces people and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, but they give little thanks; human formation and human failure stand side by side.
God creates people from clay and fixes both a life-term and an appointed term with Him, yet the addressees still doubt; earth-origin leads directly to judgment-denial.
God produced humans from earth and settled them in it, then calls them to seek forgiveness and return; earth is both origin, habitation, and setting for moral response.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are called worst in place and most astray in path, merging bodily inversion with degraded final rank.
The criminals are dragged on their faces into the Fire, a literal final lowering of bodies that rejected resurrection.
Those who bring evil are thrown face-first into the Fire; the downward bodily orientation realizes their low moral outcome.
The condemned are gathered on their faces, blind, mute, and deaf, with Hell as refuge; honored human faculties and upright carriage are comprehensively reversed.
On the day people are summoned to prostrate, they cannot do so; the once-sound upright body has lost the capacity for faithful voluntary lowering.
Eyes are humbled and humiliation covers those who were called to prostrate while sound, distinguishing chosen prostration in life from forced abasement at judgment.
When the Quran is recited, the addressees do not prostrate; refusal to lower the body before revelation becomes a sign of the deeper fall.
The next ayah identifies the refusal as denial, explicitly tying bodily non-prostration to the same تكذيب challenged in surah 95.
Those who recognize revelation fall on their faces weeping and increase in humility, completing the truthful bodily response begun in 17:107.
The command to descend to earth is followed by promised guidance and freedom from fear for those who follow it, giving the earthly descent its faithful boundary.
Those who disbelieve and deny the signs become companions of the Fire, completing the same descent passage with the opposite outcome.
Humans are sent down together, but whoever follows divine guidance will neither stray nor suffer; descent to earth does not itself determine low moral rank.
Satan is ordered to descend because proud self-exaltation has no place there and is told to leave among the abased, joining direction, arrogance, and low rank.
Good speech ascends to God and righteous action raises it, giving good deeds an upward movement opposite the denier's attachment to earth.
A building founded on reverence is opposed to one on a collapsing brink that falls with its builder into Hell; sound support and final downward collapse form the whole comparison.
A good word is a good tree whose root is firm and branch reaches heaven, a living image of upright height sustained from below and bearing continuing fruit.
An evil word is an uprooted tree with no stability in the earth, showing how loss of grounding turns apparent height into collapse.
The believers are likened to a crop that strengthens its shoots, thickens, and stands upright on its stems; mutual support produces a mature upright form.
People once stood on the brink of a pit of Fire, but God saved them as they held His rope together; divine and communal support prevent the terminal fall.
Iram is identified with lofty pillars, the very structural object named in the section as the support that holds something upright.
God wills to confer favor on those weakened in the earth and make them leaders and inheritors; the m-n-n family accompanies a divinely effected rise of the lowly into strength.
Good land brings forth vegetation by its Lord's leave while bad land yields only scant growth; the same ground bears opposed outcomes according to its condition.
A good land and forgiving Lord accompany two productive gardens and provision, showing balad as sustaining ground rather than merely a named city.
When the people turn away, their fertile gardens are replaced after the flood by bitter, sparse growth; sustaining land visibly falls from good condition.
Abraham's standing-place and the safety of whoever enters the sanctuary meet in one ayah, linking q-w-m's place-form to the secure city.
The House is made a place of return and security, and Abraham's standing-place a place of prayer; return, safety, and q-w-m converge at the sanctuary.
The Lord of the House feeds people against hunger and secures them against fear, specifying the bodily sustenance contained in the image of a secure city.
At resurrection the mountains are removed and the ground is left a level plain, stripping the standing-place of its former elevations and supports.
No crookedness or uneven rise can be seen in the leveled ground, a cosmic counterpart to removing crookedness and the final erasure of high/low terrain.
People are presented before God in rows and told they have come as first created, making first formation and final standing one explicit judicial scene.
When earth and heavens are exchanged, everyone appears before the One God; even the body's ground is remade for the final presentation.
A single blast is sufficient for resurrection, the initiating act whose bodily result appears in the next ayah.
After the blast, people are suddenly upon the earth's surface, an especially concise emergence from below to above.
The earth is stretched out before casting out what lies within it, preparing a level ground for the release described in 84:4.
The earth is shaken with its final convulsion before bringing out its burdens, so the supporting ground itself moves at bodily emergence.
The passage first identifies the one who transgressed, beginning the downward moral sequence that culminates in Fire.
Preferring the nearer life supplies the concrete choice behind the transgressor's low outcome.
Hell becomes the transgressor's refuge, the lower eschatological terminus of preferring worldly life.
The opposite person fears the standing before his Lord and restrains the self from desire; q-w-m's judicial sense produces an upright moral response.
The Garden becomes that person's refuge, completing the faithful upward alternative to 79:39.
People prefer the worldly life, a specific choice of the nearer and passing condition that parallels clinging to earth.
The Hereafter is better and more enduring, stating the lasting counterpart to the section's uncut reward.
Those content with worldly life, at rest in it, and heedless of the signs enact the earth-bound satisfaction that precedes denial's low end.
Fire is their refuge because of what they earned, completing the passage's movement from worldly contentment to final abasement.
At death the life reaches the collarbones, locating the body's loss of strength within the body itself.
One leg is entwined with the other, a vivid image of the formerly upright body's support failing at death.
On that day the drive is toward the Lord, turning bodily collapse into the unavoidable final return.
Earth is made a resting spread and sky a canopy, followed by provision; the human body's standing-place and covering are explicitly supplied by God.
Earth is made a resting-place, the broad support beneath the upright human body.
Mountains are made pegs, completing 78:6's ground with the image of what fixes and stabilizes it.
Firm mountains are cast into earth lest it shift with people, directly showing the standing-ground secured against collapse.
Firm mountains keep earth from shifting with its inhabitants, a repeated formulation of the support beneath embodied human movement.
Deniers are made to stand before their Lord, acknowledge the truth, and face punishment; rejected judgment becomes an actual presentation.
The human labors toward the Lord and will meet Him, making the body's whole exertion terminate in return and encounter.
God makes earth tractable for walking and provision, then says resurrection is to Him; the supporting ground of life leads directly to emergence.
God makes humans successors in earth and raises some over others in degrees to test them, distinguishing divinely assigned rank from moral worth.
Worldly preference already creates ranks, but the Hereafter has greater degrees and preference; final rank exceeds visible bodily and social height.
God raises Jesus and places his followers above disbelievers until resurrection, then all return for judgment; raising, rank, return, and verdict form one promise.
The deaf and speechless who do not reason are called the worst creatures before God, a moral low rank reached despite human form.
Those who refuse to hear or reason become like cattle, indeed further astray, repeating the fall beneath the rank implied by human formation.
The living and dead are not equal, and the Prophet cannot make those in graves hear; grave-ground marks a present boundary that resurrection alone will reverse.
Moses says he leans upon his staff, giving the support-object from Solomon's fall scene its ordinary bodily function.
The Fire closes upon its inmates in extended columns; a pillar that ordinarily supports becomes part of the enclosure of the fallen.
The Prophet is told not to give or remind of a favor seeking increase; this distinct m-n-n sense sets human calculated giving against God's uncut reward.
A secure sanctuary receives provision from God, repeating the safe-ground and sustenance pairing without the word balad.
The Prophet is described in relation to 'this city,' continuing 90:1's oath and locating the addressee within the same named ground; the precise nuance of حِلٌّ is not relied upon here.
People love the immediate life, naming the temporal preference behind the earthward attachment.
They leave the Hereafter, completing the boundary between passing nearness and enduring reward.
God raises some people above others in degrees so that they may take one another in service, showing social height as an interdependent support-order rather than self-sufficiency.
When Joseph's shirt reaches Jacob's face, he returns to seeing; فَٱرْتَدَّ بَصِيرًا is an exact bodily example of r-d-d restoring a prior condition.
Wealth and children are passing adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope; what passes is measured against what remains.
Enduring righteous deeds are better with God in reward and return, repeating the lasting consequence of the faithful exception.
Believers are commanded to stand before God devoutly, making created upright posture an act of worship before its final judicial form.
The servants of the Merciful spend the night prostrating and standing before their Lord, using both lowered and upright postures in faithful devotion.
